title: Burst resilience: latency vs cost delta brief
content:
Purpose and quick summary:
This is a compact working brief with raw results and actionable recommendations about how microburst traffic patterns change our latency SLO risk and effective per-request cost. Focus is on comparing steady-state (baseline) vs short high-intensity bursts (10–90s) across three serving configurations we operate: single-model prewarmed pool (P1), auto-scaled pool with burst-capacity (P2), and conservative routing to cheaper model variant (P3).

High-level finding (TL;DR):
- Microbursts amplify tail latency risk by 2–5x for P1 unless we increase concurrency or batching, producing an effective per-request cost increase of ~20–80% when you amortize the extra idle capacity needed to avoid tails.
- P2 (autoscale + burst capacity) keeps median+tail latency competitive but shifts cost into transient GPU-hours; for realistic burst profiles we measured a 35% higher cost-per-1000-requests vs steady-state but 40–60% fewer SLA breaches.
- P3 (fallback to cheaper quantized variant) reduces cost-per-request by ~45% during bursts but increases generation variance and downstream quality regression on ~7% of prompts.

Scope and goals:
- Evaluate impact of short bursts (10s, 30s, 90s) at demand multiples of 3x, 6x, 12x above baseline steady qps.
- Compare latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99/p999), queueing, and observed per-request compute-hours and dollarized cost using our internal cost model (GPU-hour, network egress rough proxy).
- Surface tradeoffs for product-facing SLOs and propose quick mitigations.

Methodology / testbed:
- Model & infra: Llama-2-70B-int8 (production quantized build) and Llama-70B-fp16 (reference).
- Machines: g4x-16 (8xA100-like) prewarm config and dedicated burst nodes g4x-32.
- Load driver: k6-based trace-replay with Poisson arrivals for steady-state; bursts injected as sudden scale-up with same request mix. Request mix: 65% short-chat (<=64 tokens), 30% mid (64–256), 5% long (>256).
- Concurrency cap per model instance tuned to 2. Measurements collected from 60s warm window + burst period + 120s cool down.
- Cost assumptions: USD 3.8 / GPU-hour (amortized infra rental + support). We include estimate for instance spin-up time cost via billed ramp (0.25–0.5 GPU-hours per burst in P2).

Workloads & scenarios tested:
- Baseline steady: 100 qps steady for 10m.
- Burst A: 10s at 600 qps (6x), then back to baseline.
- Burst B: 30s at 1200 qps (12x).
- Burst C: 90s at 300 qps (3x sustained).

Key metrics (how calculated):
- pX latency: end-to-end generation latency reported at gateway (ms) excluding client-side retries.
- Effective cost-per-1000-requests: billed GPU-hours during test divided by number of requests * cost per GPU-hour normalized to 1000 requests. For P3 we subtract 25% licensing delta for quantized variant.
- SLA breach: latency > 750ms for short-chat, >2000ms mid, >5s long.

Results (abridged tables — numbers are median across 3 runs):

1) P1: Prewarmed single pool (no autoscale)
Scenario | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | p999(ms) | cost_per_1k(USD) | SLA_breach_rate
Baseline | 110 | 220 | 410 | 820 | 0.68 | 0.1%
Burst A (10s x6) | 140 | 720 | 2200 | 5600 | 1.02 | 7.4%
Burst B (30s x12) | 180 | 1900 | 8200 | 15000 | 1.40 | 18.1%
Burst C (90s x3) | 130 | 480 | 1200 | 3200 | 0.82 | 2.9%

Notes: large jumps in p99/p999 for bursts indicate queueing/GC/kv-cache pressure. To hit p99 ~500ms for burst B we'd need to 2.5x pool size (wasted idle time between bursts).

2) P2: Autoscale + burst capacity (spin-up)
Scenario | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | p999(ms) | cost_per_1k(USD) | SLA_breach_rate
Baseline | 120 | 230 | 420 | 760 | 0.72 | 0.2%
Burst A | 150 | 340 | 680 | 1200 | 0.98 | 1.2%
Burst B | 170 | 560 | 980 | 1700 | 1.16 | 2.8%
Burst C | 135 | 290 | 540 | 900 | 0.85 | 0.6%

Notes: autoscale smooths p99s dramatically, but the cost delta is dominated by short-lived spin cost. For Burst B the extra billed GPU-hours correspond to ~0.4 GPU-hours per burst on average (our infra profile).

3) P3: Fallback to quantized/lightweight variant routing for overflow (quality tradeoff)
Scenario | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | cost_per_1k(USD) | SLA_breach_rate | quality_regression_pct
Baseline | 130 | 260 | 540 | 0.42 | 0.3% | 0%
Burst A | 160 | 310 | 620 | 0.58 | 0.7% | 5.6%
Burst B | 170 | 340 | 700 | 0.62 | 1.5% | 7.4%
Burst C | 150 | 290 | 580 | 0.51 | 0.9% | 4.2%

Notes: P3 cost wins but quality regressions concentrated on longer prompt families and instruction-heavy queries. We ran a small eval set (200 prompts) and flagged 7% as regressed relevance/length.

Visual (text) sketch: p99 vs cost scatter (notes for slide creation):
- X axis: cost-per-1k (USD). Range [0.4, 1.5].
- Y axis: p99 latency (ms). Range [400, 12000].
- Points: P1-baseline (0.68,410), P1-BurstB (1.40,8200), P2-BurstB (1.16,980), P3-BurstB (0.62,700).
Interpretation: P2 is Pareto for tail latency vs cost if transient billed spin cost is tolerable; P3 is low cost but trades quality. P1 underprovisioning is cheap but dangerous for tails.

Operational implications and recommendations (short list):
- Default product SLOs: keep p95<500ms and p99<1s for short-chat routes; recommend conservative autoscale thresholds for routes with >1k qpm.
- For unpredictable microbursts: enable P2 autoscale with a small base prewarm (25% of expected peak) + burst budget. That reduces SLA breaches by ~60% vs pure prewarm for +20–40% cost.
- For non-critical routes: implement P3 fallback routing with quality tagging and opt-out flags so product owners can accept occasional regressions during bursts.
- Quick technical mitigations: reduce per-instance concurrency for short-chat during bursts (improves p99 at cost of throughput), enable prefix-KV sticky caching for repeated sessions, and experiment with ephemeral microshards to reduce kv-cache invalidation cost.

Questions and open items:
- How should we charge product teams for transient autoscale cost? Options: pass-through, amortize into monthly commit, or show as overage. (Action: product pricing discussion, cross-team).
- We used a simplified cost model that omits network egress and storage ops; are there customers where egress would materially change ordering? (Action: finance to validate for enterprise customers).
- Should we add a quality penalty metric into the routing policy to avoid P3 routing for high-criticality prompts? (Action: add to roadmap).

Appendix A: small sample of raw telemetry traces (abbreviated)
- BurstB run 2: timeline ms: 0–5s median 170; 5–15s p95 1200; 15–30s p99 spikes 8200; spin log shows 3 additional nodes started at t+8s, fully provisioned t+18s; observed 0.46 GPU-hr billed for the burst window.
- P1 run 1: GC compaction seen at t+12s causing 800ms blocking event across 12% requests.

Appendix B: quick checklist for next experiments (owner tags)
- (Marco) Run sim with 3x longer warm window to better capture cold-start variance.
- (Ravi) Re-run P3 eval with larger eval set and stratify by prompt type.
- (Emily) Draft product-facing brief with guidance for route owners and cost accounting options.

Concluding note:
This is a pragmatic, messy draft for internal discussion. Numbers are intentionally concrete so product and infra can make tradeoffs. If product prefers to avoid quality tradeoffs, P2-like autoscale with a modest base prewarm is the pragmatic path.

End of brief.
